facts.fact: The snapshot, built on a questionnaire the Federal Vital Events Registration Agency completed in December 2018, states that only 100 kebele civil registration offices, all in the Addis Ababa City Administration, use computers to register vital events and issue certificates; it counts 18,617 kebeles, of which 16,883 (about 90 per cent, 92 per cent of them rural) had started civil registration.
facts.system: Computer registration in Addis Ababa kebele civil registration offices

facts.fact: The 100 Addis Ababa kebele offices register vital events and issue certificates on computers at the office; the snapshot describes no national electronic register, and lists a centralised electronic civil registration system as something the World Bank, Gavi and the GFF are supporting to build.
facts.system: Computer registration in Addis Ababa kebele civil registration offices

facts.fact: Outside the 100 Addis Ababa offices registration is on paper: the snapshot says paper-based registration began in most of the country in mid-2016, that the kebele records each event in a bound booklet whose copies go up to the regional office, FVERA and the CSA, and that FVERA names paper-based registration its first challenge.

The 100 computerised Addis Ababa offices are said to register 'vital events' with no event named; the snapshot gives the events the civil registration system covers as birth, marriage, divorce, death and adoption.
facts.system: Computer registration in Addis Ababa kebele civil registration offices

facts.fact: Civil registration is run by the Federal Vital Events Registration Agency under the Ministry of Peace, with regional vital events registration agencies and a civil status officer in each kebele; the organisational chart is dated 15 December 2018.

A costed five-year strategic plan for 2014 to 2018 names automation of the civil registration process as a high priority, costed at US$14,074,000 of a US$17,874,000 total (source: FVERA); FVERA had started preparing the 2019-2023 plan.

FVERA reports a government budget allocation of US$77,000 for 2014 to 2018 against an estimated plan cost of US$18 million, and an expected government allocation of US$1,407,400 towards automation, leaving a gap of US$12,666,600.

Development partners provided US$2.5 million over 2014 to 2018 (FVERA); the World Bank, Gavi and the Global Financing Facility support building a centralised electronic civil registration system and procuring office equipment, with UNICEF, UNECA, the Netherlands and UNFPA also supporting.
